item.title: A Deep Dive Into Alabama’s Reading Gains
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

A Deep Dive Into Alabama’s Reading Gains

In 2015, Alabama ranked 45th in NAEP scores. By 2024, they had climbed to 13th. Journalist Liana Loewus describes what shifted and what’s next.

In recent years, four southern states appear to be leading the way in reading growth: Mississippi, Louisiana, Tennessee and Alabama.

Decades of policy and commitment to the science of reading in Mississippi has been reported and analyzed extensively, but a new report from Thomas B. Fordham Institute continues to highlight states part of the “southern surge” — this time placing the spotlight on Alabama.

In 2015, Alabama was ranked 45th among states on the fourth grade National Assessment of Educational Progress, but in the years that followed rose to 18th in 2019 and 13th in 2024.

In a 42-page study, journalist Liana Loewus reports the history of Alabama reading policy, looking back at over three decades of initiatives, including a failed expansion in the 2000s resulting in pulling back efforts and a reinvestment in literacy coaches, curriculum and intervention since 2019.

Alabama “has been one of the few states to show academic improvement over the last two rounds of NAEP,” Loewus wrote in the report. “After falling below the national average for fourth-grade reading between 2013 and 2022, the state is closing the gap again. Its 2024 average scale score was … just two points below the national average.”

In an interview with The 74, Loewus spoke in depth about her findings and the state’s next steps.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I’ll kick off our conversation by asking you to summarize your findings with this report, mainly about Alabama’s early adoption of literacy reforms, what went wrong and where we’re at now.

A: The Alabama story is just so fascinating. You can really see the beginning and trajectory and follow the line very clearly between policy implementation and impact on students.

Alabama is still not at the top, but they were making gains when no one else was, even staying steady when the pandemic hit and it was important to look at why.

The story really starts 30 years ago when Catherine Mitchell, after working in the Alabama State Department of Ed for nearly 20 years, took over literacy in 1998. She raised $1.5 million with two unlikely allies, A+ Education Partnership, a progressive advocacy group and the Eagle Forum, a very conservative group, who all agreed they wanted to teach kids how to read, launching a program that became the Alabama Reading Initiative.

It started with 16 schools. Mitchell said ‘Give me your non-readers, and we’re going to teach them how to read,’ and she will say no one in Alabama knew anything about phonics at that time. She had to write training modules for the teachers about phonics and phonemic awareness. She hired teachers who knew about comprehension, teaching kids how to understand what they were reading and language comprehension. At the end of the year, the data was really good, there were fewer referrals to special education and reading scores went up.

She went back and got the state legislature to fund $6 million. By the mid 2000s, a literacy coach who was trained by the Alabama Reading Initiative, an arm of the Department of Education, was put in every single K-3 school. Between 2005 to 2007, fourth grade reading scores jumped more than any other state. They were basically on par with the national average by 2011, which was pretty important for them because they had been far below for a long time.

In 2012, the state superintendent at the time decided to expand on the coaching initiative; they’d decided to bring coaches to all schools, K-12, and other subjects but there was less training. The whole initiative was watered down, ARI funding went from $58 million in 2013 to $40.7 million by 2018 — funding went down but the initiative had expanded.

In 2018, Mississippi started to get attention, and there’s a little bit of next door rivalry, so leaders in Alabama, including Rep. Terry Collins went to Mississippi to find out what’s happening. Collins became convinced that Alabama needed a law like Mississippi’s 2013 Literacy Based Promotion Act, pushing really hard for comprehensive literacy law.

The law passed in 2019 with flying colors. This year, ARI is funded at $152 million.

At The 74, we launched the Bright Spots series, highlighting schools that are beating the odds in literacy. In Connecticut, a district talked about three things: accountability, coaching and curriculum, which aligned with your report and three main things you’ve taken out of Alabama. Which of those three would you say has had the greatest impact?

Coaching is a huge piece of it.

It’s extremely prescriptive, Alabama ensures that all coaches are trained in the same way and they all have the same base knowledge. The state also gives every single school $85,000 for a literacy coach, where in a lot of places, they’ll say you need coaches and it’s unfunded.

I think the most important thing that Alabama does is they wrote into the law that these coaches have to focus on coaching. They wrote a list of things these coaches cannot do. They can work with teachers and sometimes with students, but they cannot do extra recess and administrative duties. They cannot fill in as subs, they can’t be pulled for other things.

Another thing I learned that has a large impact is having steady leadership that is committed to research-based practices and hires people who really understand it. We had Terry Collins, Dr. Mackey and Gov. Kate Ivey. Dr. Mackey has been in office for nearly nine years at this point. Terry Collins was in the legislature for 15 years. They’ve stuck with the policy, they’ve stayed the course and that’s a big deal.…

item.title: LAUSD Spent Over $6 Million on a Phone Ban. Survey Data Show Mixed Results
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

LAUSD Spent Over $6 Million on a Phone Ban. Survey Data Show Mixed Results

In the first district-wide survey since the policy began, students and staff did agree that engagement has improved.

A majority of students are complying with Los Angeles Unified’s cellphone ban and paying more attention in class, at least according to school staff.

That’s one finding from the first survey of students and staff to include questions about bell-to-bell restrictions implemented in February 2025.

“It’s a big difference in terms of [students’] ability and willingness to focus on whatever we’re doing in class,” said Elizabeth Ruff, an English teacher at Garfield High School. “Obviously there are always some kids who are distracted … even if it’s not their phone. But that has decreased a lot really, really markedly.”

But there are still unanswered questions about what effect, if any, LAUSD’s student phone-use restrictions have on student learning and behavior, including recent gains on state tests.

Compliance varies, too: Middle school staff estimated that two-thirds of students “mostly” abided by the restrictions. Among high school staff, that number dropped to just over half.

More than 160,000 students answered the survey, as did more than 21,000 staff members.

The results of the spring 2026 School Experience Survey, which queries staff, students and parents on a number of topics, are the first public, quantitative measure of how LAUSD’s updated cellphone policy has changed student behavior on campus. While some survey answers are available online, results of the questions specific to the cellphone policy were released to LAist only upon request.

LAUSD’s policy predated the state of California’s requirements for all schools to restrict student cellphones by July 2026. At least 40 states and the District of Columbia have similar restrictions, according to Education Week, largely based on the premise that phones and social media distract students from learning and amplify conflicts, among other concerns.

How middle and high school students differ

LAUSD middle and high school students are split nearly evenly on whether the policy improved their focus in class.

Myson Thomas, 17, is a senior at King/Drew Magnet High School. He said he doesn’t use his school’s magnetically sealed Yondr pouches, but he also isn’t on his phone in class.

“I’m at school to learn, so I’m gonna turn my phone off,” Thomas said. “I already take rigorous courses, so it’s no point of me using my phone at school.”

Fewer than half of high school students reported they focused better in class all or most of the time without their phone compared to nearly 58% of their peers in middle school.

“In implementing a phone-free policy across the district, we recognized that changing long-standing habits would take time,” a district spokesperson said in a statement to LAist. “We recognize there is still work to do and will continue listening to students, families and staff as we refine our approach to support focused learning and meaningful in-person connections.”

Board Member Nick Melvoin, who co-sponsored the cellphone policy, said he was “really encouraged” that most middle and high school student respondents said they were interacting with each other more without their phones.

“This isn’t just about trying to be punitive adults,” Melvoin said. “This is about [students] having a much more engaging day, a more fulfilling day when you’re not just scrolling or texting.”

How we got here

LAUSD joined a growing number of districts and states clamping down on student cellphone use in June 2024 when the school board voted to extend the existing class-time ban to include lunch and passing periods.

Board members cited concerns about the effect of phones and social media on youth mental health, bullying and distraction from classroom instruction.

Educators who spoke in support of stricter rules said their schools had few resources or administrative support to enforce the existing rules and said that policing phone use ate up time and created conflicts with students.

“It definitely felt a little bit like playing Whac-A-Mole in terms of trying to do everything else I’m supposed to be doing in the classroom and also be looking out for who secretly has a cellphone behind their book,” said Ruff, the Garfield High School teacher.

How LAUSD enforced phone restrictions

The board’s vote allocated $7 million to implement the policy. Schools could choose whether they wanted to purchase pouches or lockers to store students’ phones or rely on the “honor system,” and ask students to keep their devices powered off and in their backpacks.

About half of schools purchased devices to enforce the ban, according to a district spokesperson at the time the policy went into effect.

Documents provided to LAist through a public records request show LAUSD spent about $6.35 million on products related to cellphone policy implementation during the 2024-25 school year. Of that, the district spent $5.42 million on Yondr products (including phone pouches) and nearly $930,000 on products from Amazon, including phone lockers.

What we know about the effectiveness of phone restrictions

LAist first spoke to Miles, a student at the Sherman Oaks Center for Enriched Studies, when the restrictions began in 2025. At the time, he called the phone-free policy “really, really annoying.”

“I think it’s still a pretty useless policy,” Miles, now a junior, said. ”It doesn’t change anything other than how we hide our phones.”

LAist agreed not to publish Miles’ last name to protect his privacy.

He, like Thomas, said he doesn’t use his school’s phone storage pouches and doesn’t use his phone in class.

Students have also reportedly circumvented the pouches by storing a dummy phone or breaking open the locks.…

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-21 11:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.

The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.

But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.

Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.

“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.

Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.

The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.

In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”

His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.

The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.

Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.

Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.

The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.

To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.

Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.

In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.

“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-18 02:03 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/south-korea-university-entrace-exams-ai-cheating-measures

item.title: NYC Public School Enrollment Drops, Raising Questions Over Budgets and Closures
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

NYC Public School Enrollment Drops, Raising Questions Over Budgets and Closures

Public schools have lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers from the Education Department.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

New York City’s public schools lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers the Education Department released Monday.

That leaves the nation’s largest school system with about 766,900 students, from kindergarten through senior year, as of Oct. 31, with several contributing factors leading to the drop: falling birth rates, families leaving the city, and a slowdown of immigration into the five boroughs under President Donald Trump.

Over the past decade, the city has lost about 200,000 students, or nearly 20%.

Enrollment in city-funded preschool programs was up slightly, thanks to the rollout of a new program for 2,000 2-year-olds this year as well as an uptick in 4-year-olds signed up for prekindergarten programs.

What the dip means for school budgets remains murky. Historically, when schools have fewer students than projected on their roster, the Education Department claws back money in the middle of the school year. But since the pandemic, the city has largely kept school budgets steady despite enrollment declines. Officials declined to say whether they planned to continue that policy, known as being “held harmless.” Since 2020, New York City has spent nearly $2 billion to prop up budgets at schools with declining enrollment.

Any changes to wind down that policy could be politically explosive, as schools could have to cut back on after-school and other enrichment programs this school year and eventually let go of teachers. When former Mayor Eric Adams proposed phasing it out, the blowback was so intense that City Council members apologized for giving him the green light. (The decision was later rolled back.)

In his first budget deal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani kept school budgets whole, though some experts warn that approach is inequitable because it allows schools with declining enrollment to spend significantly more per student than other campuses.

Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has repeatedly raised concerns about declining enrollment, saying that the city will need to look closer at closures or mergers for schools too small to offer a full array of courses. Already, the city is floating proposals to close two small schools in Harlem and one in Brooklyn, as well as merge two sets of schools in the Bronx and Brooklyn, according to public documents. Those plans are expected to be voted on by the Panel for Educational Policy over the next two months.

“We’ve started to have conversations in communities,” Samuels told the Chancellor’s Parent Advisory Committee last week. “It doesn’t mean it’s not going to be tough sometimes, but they have been going pretty well.”

Enrollment is projected to continue declining. By the 2034-35 school year, the city is predicting that the student population will fall by another 130,000, according to demographic projections from the School Construction Authority.

The declines in New York City mirror national trends. Thirty states have seen public school enrollment declines since 2014. Many large school systems — including in Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Houston — are also grappling with sharp drops.

Mamdani’s administration pointed to some efforts to help bolster city schools, including reducing class sizes, which is required by state law and has likely been aided by declining student headcounts. Aside from continuing some of his predecessor’s initiatives, Mamdani has yet to articulate a vision for the public school system. He has focused more on his affordability agenda and expanding his free 2-K program, which expects to add 10,000 more seats next year.

When the city’s free preschool programs for 2-, 3-, and 4-year-olds are included in the enrollment tally, the total is 863,100, according to the Education Department’s preliminary data. That was down about 2.6% from the previous year.

Chalkbeat New York Reporter Michael Elsen-Rooney contributed.

Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools. This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters

item.title: Macron banned smartphones in schools. A month later, France was ablaze. Could they be connected? | Joseph de Weck
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

Remember the 1999 blockbuster The Matrix? It may be more than a quarter of a century old, but it has become a byword and a meme for a frighteningly plausible kind of 21st-century tech dystopia.

A quick recap: the computer hacker Neo discovers that machines rule over humanity. They keep people trapped in pods, their minds immersed in a virtual reality designed to keep them docile (the “Matrix” of the title). Once he becomes aware of the world he actually inhabits, Neo decides to take up arms.

Is that the kind of awakening France’s youth is experiencing today? Could a government-mandated digital detox have had the unintended consequence of protests and riots on such a scale that the army was brought out on to the streets?

This October, hundreds of thousands of French youngsters walked out of school and joined mass protests. Their demands include fixing France’s moribund school infrastructure and restoring every graduate’s right to choose their university and degree programme. Above all, they want to revive the école de la République, France’s public school system, as the engine of social mobility. Today only sport stars, crypto bros and influencers seem to be getting ahead in life.

These problems are nothing new. But what has triggered a reaction on this scale now?

Mara Goyet, a teacher in Paris, argues that the phone ban in lycées, introduced in September, helped spark the uprising. Suddenly disconnected from their own matrix, the pupils raised their eyes from their phone screens and could no longer tune out the grim reality of the world they inhabit, Goyet writes.

Emmanuel Macron decided to make the war on les écrans – screens – a legacy of his botched second term.

In 2024, the Élysée Palace asked a panel of experts, including neurologists and psychiatrists, to analyse the effects of digital technology on youth. It found that young French people aged 16 to 19 spent more than five hours a day staring at their phones. Shortened attention spans, a sedentary lifestyle and mental health issues were the consequence, the panel found.

Following the report, on 21 July the national assembly passed a law restricting social media access for under-15s and banning phones in lycées, coming into effect for the new school year. Perhaps paradoxically, the leftwing France Insoumise (LFI) had voted against the law, denouncing it as “a form of digital paternalism”. The far-right Rassemblement National abstained.

The constitutional court quickly overturned the social media ban. But when teenagers returned from their summer holidays, teachers were asking them to leave their phone in lockers or put them in sealed pouches.

A teacher working in a Parisian suburb, writing anonymously in Le Grand Continent, describes a classroom transformed: “As soon as the class, with its necessary tyranny, came to an end, the brains switched off. The 30 or so brains were drained by the image drug. My class became a group of zombies … This year, without their phones, my students are more lively, more engaging, more engaging, more disorganised, more excitable, more childlike. They’re also more of a pain.”

Another teacher told me much the same story: with the arrival of smartphones, breaktimes had grown quieter, with many pupils absorbed by their TikTok feed or playing games. Now, the hallways are loud again, buzzing with life.

For a shared political consciousness to form, people need to break out of isolation, talk to one another and build trust. That seems to have happened. And for pupils pushed back into the analogue world, political action goes beyond online posting and out into the streets.

Appropriately, the trigger for the French student movement that erupted into the era-defining protests of May 1968 was another interdiction: a ban on female and male students spending the night together in dormitories at the Nanterre campus, University of Paris.

By protesting as their forebears did in 68, today’s students also briefly disrupted what Guy Debord described as the “society of the spectacle”: a world in which reality is shaped by a flood of images, performative acts and mediated information. Here, by contrast, was the direct experience of reality. Standing together in the clouds of teargas that engulfed Paris and other cities on 17 October, a new generation of French citizens forged a collective lived experience that showed them they could be actors, not just spectators of political life.

Sociologists will have to study whether the enforced digital detox has really helped trigger this movement. After all, pupils have also organised their actions via social media, and the protests are extensively live-streamed on the same smartphones and platforms they have been detached from at school. This is a hybrid uprising.

But one thing is already clear. Students are not taking to the streets because they want to overturn the phone ban.

Louis Letoublon, vice-president of Les Lycéens!, an organisation of high school students, says: “The phone ban is unbearable, as it infantilises the students.” Some protest posters read: “Adult and vaccinated, but I am still getting my phone taken away at school.” Or: “You can take away my phone, but not my voice.”

But the government has set up a platform where pupils can register their demands. According to preliminary results based on more than 60,000 contributions, 70% said school days were too long, and 48.2% cited poor infrastructure, particularly the cold in winter and heat in summer. Only 9% of students demanded that the phone ban be overturned.

France’s young people took to the streets because they want better schools, not because they see Macron as an overbearing father, confiscating phones as punishment.

Two years ago, Macron declared that it was urgent to “retake control of our screens, that too often enclose us, where they should liberate us”. The irony is that, by unplugging teenagers from the matrix, he may have unleashed a storm that has sealed his decline and fall.…

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-18 05:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

MIDDLEBURY, Vt.

There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants about a classmate who spent a semester learning how to forage in Malaysia.

Middlebury College looks and sounds … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it’s working hard to persuade people that it’s not.

Middlebury has announced that, starting next year, students from families with annual household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free. It becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make this kind of promise, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

These may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation’s median household income. But while it’s true that few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people in those earnings categories already attend without having to pay tuition.

When families see these pronouncements, they think, “ ‘Oh, wow, the college is cutting the price.’ And that’s almost a perfect example of the misperceptions of the pricing system,” said Phillip Levine, an economist at Wellesley College who studies higher education finance and is the author of the book “Hidden Tuition: An Insider’s Guide to College Pricing and Financial Aid.”

In fact, said Levine, whose research bears this out, at most of the institutions making these tuition-free guarantees, “the college was already free for almost all those kids.”

The real purpose of what Middlebury and other schools are doing, he and other experts say, is to solve a problem that has soured many Americans on higher education: how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what college will cost.

“Let’s make it as non-complicated as possible,” said Ian Baucom, president at Middlebury: “If your family income is $175,000 or less, at Middlebury, you don’t pay tuition.” What the school is doing, he said, is trying to “just [be] really clear and get that out of the way, and then let the students decide.”

Most of the growing number of income-based tuition plans take effect next year, as at Middlebury, or began for students who enrolled this fall.

That’s not coincidental. Many of these schools have reached or surpassed a listed price of attendance of $100,000 a year; at Middlebury, it’s $97,386. And public confusion about how much they actually cost after discounts and financial aid is helping drive a near-record-low confidence in higher education that threatens to exacerbate enrollment and revenue challenges.

Nearly 70 percent of students and parents think the financial aid process is partly or completely confusing, according to a separate survey by the Strada Education Foundation.

Most Americans also think that colleges are overpriced, with nearly two-thirds saying four-year institutions are unaffordable, a Gallup survey found; among parents who don’t want their children to go to a four-year college, it found, the biggest reason was the cost.

Related: Some colleges aim financial aid at a declining market: Students in the middle class

A culprit for this is colleges’ own increasingly self-destructive policy of advertising a high list price that almost no one pays, then giving discounts. It’s a strategy that has evolved from a time when the price was intended to signal value and the discounts — which the colleges call “scholarships” — to entice the most desirable prospective students to enroll.

Guarantees do not include room, board and other expenses, though separate financial aid is often available for those.

Source: The Hechinger Report | Published: 2026-11-13 14:33 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
item.description:

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories

Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.

An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.

Many parents do not.

"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.

But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.

A baffling move

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.

She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.

Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.

"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."

When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.

NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.

The "AI or nothing" approach

In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.

The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.

Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.

"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.

Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.

He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.

"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."

The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

item.title: Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: real reporting, concrete detail

According to the Association of American Colleges and Universities, active learning is an essential part of a modern college education. High Impact Practices (HIPs) use collaborative and active learning strategies to improve student engagements and outcomes. White (2018) explained that while HIPs can positively impact student success, budgetary restraints can present challenges to implementation. Therefore, faculty are finding ways to create active learning experiences without a high cost to institutions.

Cross-disciplinary collaboration presents an opportunity to use HIPs to engage students in the core curriculum. In my case, the First-Year Writing (FYW) classroom offers a unique setting to use HIPs to build on how writing creates common spaces not only in FYW, but also expands those spaces into discipline-specific areas, such as nursing. Cross-disciplinary collaboration through FYW not only provides students with an early look at their majors but also teaches them how to decompartmentalize the writing skills they learn in FYW and apply them to a broader experience.

This article will focus on one such collaboration between English (English 1101) and Nursing and the impact of cross-disciplinary activities and HIPs on students in a discipline-specific FYW course.

Importance of Collaboration

Collaborative projects can provide students with deeper learning experiences and opportunities for increasing communication (written and oral) skills both inside the classroom and within the community (White, 2018; Bresciani, 2015). The FYW classroom provides a unique setting to build on momentum in cases where students are unable to have an early introduction to their major. FYW challenges students to understand the connection of strong writing to their majors, especially if the material in the course correlates to relevant subject matter in the major. The goal in creating this cost-effective nursing-specific English 1101 was to ask students to think specifically about how writing relates to a more universal experience (medical professions) in order to express the importance of humanities beyond the composition classroom.

Collaboration, particularly in course design and implementation, can often seem like a heavy lift. In some cases, faculty can be protective of course material and design, and in others, challenges exist in finding partnerships outside of specific disciplinary departments. In the following, I hope to show how this type of critical work can happen organically and effectively while bringing satisfaction and appreciation not only to students but to the faculty involved.

Process of Implementation

Over the course of a semester and over the summer, I worked with a nursing faculty member to refine the necessary concepts for bringing the course into the classroom. I started with the basic course learning outcomes for our institution’s English 1101.

From there, I and my nursing faculty partner, explored what concepts would be important for students interested in the nursing program to learn early in their academic careers. I began with highlighting the connection between the humanities and health care through learning about and constructing a medical narrative where students had to articulate their interest in pursuing a nursing career. Then, I focused on the importance of communication in relaying critical information through instructions by creating a process project, which included a demonstration (by my nursing partner) of a Foley catheter insertion using a medical mannequin, followed by a hands-on opportunity for students to practice this foundational healthcare procedure. Finally, I had students hone their research skills by exploring relevant and current healthcare-related issues and presenting them in a multimedia assignment. Instead of MLA, as is common in most humanities courses, students used APA formatting and citations throughout the course to better prepare them for the nursing program.

Please scan the QR code below for copies of the assignments.

Lessons Learned and Advice

Engagement

Students were more motivated to engage with assignments. They appreciated exposure to nursing concepts early in their academic careers and enjoyed forming an early relationship with a nursing faculty member. The course sparked their intellectual curiosity and got them thinking about the deeper issues within their major and future profession. When learning is decompartmentalized, students can see connection between academic and life experiences. Potential nursing students expressed excitement for discipline-specific core classes and, sometimes, students realized that the hands-on activities showed them that nursing was not their best fit, well before they spent years working towards acceptance into the nursing program.

Collaboration

Collaboration opportunities don’t have to be complicated, expensive, or overly time-consuming. Simple conversations and activities can be cost-effective while academically sound and engaging. Partnerships can happen in surprising situations. The nursing English 1101 collaboration started as a kernel of an idea while riding in the back of a college-issued Ford Taurus on the way home from a teaching and learning conference. It’s important to note that collaborative course work should involve immediate supervisors (chairs and deans), advisors, and the Registrar. In my situation, we needed to make sure the course was populated with future nursing students, which would be information the Registrar provided and advisors actively used for registration.
